analysis.one_liner: Requires nearly all employers to give workers earned paid sick time, plus 14 extra days during a public health emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the first days of the COVID-19 pandemic but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require every employer, from the largest company down to a business with a single employee, to let workers earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours (7 days) a year. It would cover the worker's own illness, care for a sick family member, appointments, school closures, and leave for domestic violence or stalking victims. When a public health emergency is declared, employers would have to immediately provide 14 additional paid days to full-time workers and the equivalent for part-time workers, usable right away regardless of how long the person had been on the job. It was introduced on March 9, 2020, as COVID-19 was spreading, and died in committee at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of workers, especially hourly and part-time workers in restaurants, retail, and care work, who at the time often had no paid sick days at all. It also protects survivors of domestic violence and workers whose children's schools close during an emergency.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly and part-time workers without sick leave

how_it_helps.text: Workers earn 1 hour of paid sick time per 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours (7 days) per year, usable for their own illness, preventive care, or care for a child, spouse, domestic partner, parent, or other close family member.

When a public health emergency is declared, workers get an immediate 14 days of additional paid sick time (full-time salaried) or their scheduled hours over 14 days (part-time and hourly), usable right away with no waiting period and no doctor's note required during the emergency.

Paid sick time may be used when a workplace is closed by public order, when the worker has been exposed to a communicable disease and may pose a risk to others, or when a child's school or care place is closed during an emergency.

Time may also be used for medical care, counseling, relocation, or legal proceedings related to domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking, with confidentiality protections, and employers are barred from firing or retaliating against workers who use it.
The paid time must be compensated at no less than the worker's regular rate, the federal minimum wage, or the applicable state or local minimum wage, whichever is highest.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who must fund the accrued days and the 14-day emergency leave out of their own payrolls, with no federal reimbursement or tax credit. The burden falls hardest on small businesses and industries like restaurants and retail that run on thin margins and hourly scheduling.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers of all sizes, especially small businesses

drawbacks.text: The mandate carries no federal subsidy, tax credit, or reimbursement, so employers — including the smallest businesses with a single employee — bear the full payroll cost, and the 14-day emergency leave obligation takes effect immediately on the day an emergency is declared, with compliance required before regulations are even written.

Because the bill covers any employer with one or more employees, even very small firms that many paid-leave proposals exempt would face the full requirement, which an honest supporter would acknowledge is a real cost in low-margin sectors.

Employers with existing generous policies are not required to add more, and workers are not paid out for unused accrued time when they leave a job, so the bill builds a floor rather than expanding leave for workers who already have it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is large and concrete: guaranteed paid time to see a doctor, recover, or care for a child without losing pay — precisely what public health guidance says stops the spread of disease in a pandemic. The cost is a real, unfunded payroll mandate on employers, concentrated on small and low-margin businesses, and the bill's immediate effective date with no subsidies would have been difficult to absorb mid-crisis. A design that paired the mandate with federal reimbursement for small employers would have softened that trade-off; this bill chose universality and speed instead.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced, none of which ever held a hearing or vote on it, and the House never brought it to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on March 9, 2020, days before the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, and it was referred the same day to the Education and Labor, House Administration, Oversight and Reform, and Judiciary Committees.
The action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.
Eighty-three House Democrats cosponsored the bill, all from the majority party, but no Republican cosponsor appears in the record.

Instead of this comprehensive bill, Congress enacted a narrower emergency response, the Families First Coronavirus Response Act, which provided two weeks of paid sick leave during the pandemic but only to workers at employers with fewer than 500 employees, leaving workers at large companies uncovered.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, particularly larger companies and low-wage industries, avoided the full cost of a permanent, universal paid sick time mandate, and in the pandemic response avoided covering their own workers' emergency leave.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided a paid-leave mandate

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 9, 2020, during the first days of the COVID-19 outbreak.

against.name: Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of primary jurisdiction, took no action on the bill after its referral; the record shows no hearing, markup, or committee vote.

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; the House instead passed the narrower Families First Coronavirus Response Act, which limited emergency paid sick leave to workers at employers with fewer than 500 employees.

sides.party_line_note: All 84 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, no Republican cosponsor appears in the record, and with Democrats holding the House majority and controlling its calendar, the bill's fate was decided by members of the sponsoring party.

industries.industry: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage hourly service employers
industries.note: These employers would bear the full cost of paid sick time for workers who often had none, including 14 extra emergency days with no reimbursement. Their interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the workers' interest in having it.

industries.industry: Employers of all sizes, including very small businesses
industries.note: The bill covers any employer with one or more employees, exempting no one, and required compliance immediately upon enactment during an emergency without waiting for regulations. The cost falls on payroll, in competing against businesses that already paid for leave only if the floor is enforced equally.

industries.industry: State and local governments and public agencies
industries.note: Public agencies are treated as covered employers, so government units would owe the same paid sick time to their workers as private firms.
